overview: PhysBox: Etch (etch.physbox.io) is a 2D vector CAD & manufacturing studio for laser cutting, vector etching, and CNC milling/carving. The document model is SVG-native and measured in millimetres: a document is a piece of stock (width x height, material, stockThickness) carrying layers (cut / etch / fill / shade) and elements (rect, circle, ellipse, line, polygon, star, text, symbol, bezier, freehand, path, image). It supports Google Fonts text, a clip-art symbol library, parametric mandala & radial symmetry tools, raster image import in four modes (traced vector, halftone, scanline, greyscale shade), and direct GRBL/Marlin G-code toolpath export with Web Serial streaming.
workflow: 1. Call etch_get_schema for the document/element/layer schema and preset list, then etch_get_state to see the document currently on the canvas.

2. Call etch_list_capabilities for what this machine actually has — its tool rack, the material list, the layer operations and the image modes. The rack is user-editable, so advising a tool from memory advises fitting one they may not own.
3. Set up the job with etch_set_document (stock size, material, stockThickness, machine, layers) — fields you omit are kept from the current document.

4. Build geometry: etch_add_element for one shape at a time, etch_set_svg to drop a whole SVG onto the canvas at once, etch_add_clipart to place a library symbol (etch_list_clipart names them), or etch_add_image to bring in a raster picture, then etch_combine to cut one shape out of another — that is how a plate with a slot or a bracket with a bite taken out of it gets made, rather than by drawing the outline by hand.
5. Change one shape with etch_update_element rather than resending the whole elements array — a wholesale write discards anything that moved in between.
6. Or start from a template with etch_list_presets and etch_load_preset — note that loading a preset replaces the whole document.

7. On an unfamiliar material, offer etch_make_test_grid before the real job: it cuts a square per speed/power combination so the settings come from measurement rather than from the feeds model's estimate. It replaces the open document, so say so first.

8. Set the note card with etch_set_note_card once the geometry is final — what the piece is, its finished size in mm, the stock it is cut from, and what each layer does. The job is not finished without it.
9. Export with etch_export_svg (clean SVG XML) or etch_generate_gcode (GRBL/Marlin toolpath, inner-contour-first, kerf-compensated).
10. While a job runs, etch_machine_status reports progress and etch_machine_trim nudges feed or power if the user says it is cutting too hot or too slow. Neither can start or stop anything.
11. Before generating G-code, call etch_validate_document — off-stock geometry, dead layer references and shallow cuts all export without complaint.
12. etch_get_screenshot shows you what you drew; etch_get_summary is the cheap numeric read of the same thing.
gotchas: THE BRIDGE IS A LOCAL HUB, NOT THE DEV SERVER: Etch dials the physbox_mcp hub on ws://localhost:3142 directly, so these tools work against a hosted build as well as a local one — what has to be running is the hub and a browser tab with Etch open in it. Nothing reaches a tab that is closed.

EVERYTHING IS MILLIMETRES, ORIGIN TOP-LEFT: x increases right, y increases down, from the top-left corner of the stock. The document's `origin` field ('top-left' | 'center' | 'bottom-left') controls where machine X0 Y0 sits for the G-code, not where the canvas draws.

ELEMENT x/y IS THE LOCAL ORIGIN, AND WHERE THAT SITS DEPENDS ON THE TYPE: circle and ellipse are drawn about it (x/y is the centre); rect is drawn from it (x/y is the top-left corner); line starts there and ends at x2/y2 relative to it; text hangs down from it; polygon/star/path/symbol are drawn from it in their own local coordinates. Rotation always pivots about the element's own bounding-box centre.

PARTIAL DOCUMENTS ARE MERGED, PRESETS ARE NOT: etch_set_document merges the fields you send onto the current document, so sending only {width, height} resizes the stock and keeps the drawing. etch_load_preset replaces the document outright — anything unsaved on the canvas is gone.

ELEMENTS NEED A LAYER THAT EXISTS: layerId defaults to 'cut'. If you sent a document whose layers do not include that id, the element will not be machined. The stock two layers are 'cut' (through-cut contours) and 'etch' (surface engraving).

SIZE FIELDS ARE PER TYPE: rect uses w/h (rx/ry for corner radius), circle uses r, ellipse uses rx2/ry2, line uses x2/y2, polygon uses points, text uses text/fontSize/fontFamily, path/bezier/freehand use d or bezierNodes. Sending w/h on a circle does nothing.

STAR AND PATH ARE DRAWN FROM `d`: etch_add_element stores what you send verbatim, so an element of those types with no `d` renders and machines as nothing. Send explicit SVG path data, or use rect/circle/ellipse/line/polygon, which are generated from their own fields. A `symbol` is the exception: send a symbolId from etch_list_clipart and the path data is filled in from the library.

MACHINE KIND DECIDES WHETHER Z EXISTS: document.machine 'laser' modulates power at a fixed height and ignores per-layer zDepth; 'cnc' cuts in passes to zDepth. Set material and stockThickness — feeds, spindle speed and depth-per-pass are all derived from them, and 'cut through' is meaningless without a thickness.
KERF IS NOT OPTIONAL: contour offset is applied by default so parts come out to size; opt out per element with cutSide 'on' rather than by disabling it globally.

TEXT IS OUTLINED BEFORE IT IS CUT: a text element machines from its generated outline, which is regenerated when the text or font changes. A font that has not loaded yet can briefly outline differently from what the canvas shows.

AN IMAGE IS TONE, NOT A SHAPE: etch_add_image has four modes. 'vector' traces an outline, 'halftone' makes a dot grid and 'scanline' makes engrave lines — all three decide at import that a pixel is either cut or not, and land as one compound path element. 'shade' does not: it puts the greyscale pixels in the document as an `image` element and lets darkness vary along the move, so pitch, angle, depth and size stay editable afterwards. Shading needs a layer whose operation is 'shade' — the import makes one if the document has none, and the planner skips an image on any other kind of layer.
ONLY IMAGE BYTES, NOT URLS: etch_add_image takes base64 (or a data: URL). A remote URL drawn into a canvas taints it and the pixels become unreadable, so an http source cannot work.

CLIP ART IS PLACED BY ID: etch_add_clipart (or etch_add_element with type 'symbol' and a symbolId) fills in the path data and the viewBox scale for you. The library mixes a legacy 24-unit grid with a newer 100-unit one, so a symbol assembled by hand with a fixed scale comes out four times the size of its neighbours.
TEXT IS OUTLINED FOR YOU: add a `text` element with text/fontSize/fontFamily and the app vectorizes it — any Google Font. Do not send letterforms as path data.

BOOLEANS CONSUME THEIR INPUTS, AND ORDER DECIDES THE RESULT: etch_combine's first element id is the base and the rest act on it, so a subtract done the other way round keeps the offcut and destroys the part. The inputs are removed from the document; one undo in the UI brings them back. Open paths cannot take part and are left where they were.

A COMBINE THAT LEAVES SPECKS MEANS THE SHAPES DID NOT LINE UP: hairlines thinner than 0.05 mm are dropped as arithmetic noise, but a leftover of, say, 0.3 mm is real geometry and is kept and reported in the note. It is nearly always two edges meant to be flush and drawn a fraction of a millimetre apart — move them together and combine again rather than deleting the speck.

THE TEST GRID REPLACES THE DOCUMENT: etch_make_test_grid is not an addition to the drawing. Call etch_get_state and keep the result first if the current document matters, or tell the user what is about to happen.

CUT OUT THE SUBJECT WITH options.cutout, NOT WITH A SECOND IMPORT: for a photo of someone against a plain white or black backdrop, etch_add_image with cutout true finds the backdrop from the picture's edges, ignores it, puts one closed outline around what is left on the cut layer (making one if the document has none), and applies the chosen mode to the subject only — 'shade' for a photograph, 'vector' for a logo. The outline is a flood fill from the edges, so a white shirt on a white wall stays inside it. The two elements are placed at the same x/y and must be moved together.

DITHERING IS FOR SHADE MODE ONLY: the other three image modes threshold the picture, and handing a thresholder an already-dithered image traces the dot pattern itself — tens of thousands of tiny loops instead of an outline.

YOU CANNOT START THE MACHINE: etch_machine_trim adjusts a job already running and etch_machine_status reads it, and that is the whole machine surface. Homing, jogging, zeroing, framing and running are done by the person standing next to the machine, in the app. Ask them to press it; do not look for a tool that does it.
coordinateSystem: Millimetres, origin at the top-left of the stock, x right and y down. An element's geometry is drawn in its own local coordinates and then translated by x/y, scaled by scaleX/scaleY and rotated by `rotation` degrees clockwise about its bounding-box centre — so x/y is the centre of a circle but the top-left corner of a rect. Default stock is 300 x 200 mm.

tools.etch_add_clipart: Place a clip-art symbol by id. Path data and the per-symbol viewBox scale are filled in for you; x/y default to centred on the stock and `size` to a bounding size that fits it. Returns the new element's id and the size used.
tools.etch_add_element: Add one vector shape, text, path, symbol or image to the canvas. Only `type` is really needed; x/y default to the centre of the stock, layerId to 'cut', and stroke/fill to the cut-layer defaults. A `symbol` sent with a symbolId and no `d` is resolved from the clip-art library. Returns the new element's id.
tools.etch_add_image: Import a raster image (base64 or data: URL) in one of four modes: 'vector' (marching-squares outline trace), 'halftone' (dot grid), 'scanline' (engraved lines) or 'shade' (greyscale tone). `options` accepts mode, threshold, brightness, contrast, gamma, invert, dither, smoothing, targetWidth, targetHeight, halftoneSpacing, scanlineSpacing, shadePitch, simplifyPx, and cutout (with cutoutBackground, cutoutTolerance, cutoutSmoothPx); sizes default to an aspect-preserving fit on the stock. A shade import lands on a shade layer, creating one if the document has none. With cutout, the backdrop is removed and its edge is added as a second element on a cut layer. Returns the new element's id, the layer it landed on, any shade or cut layer created, and outlineId when a cutout was made.
tools.etch_add_registration: Add registration holes — the pin holes a stack of sheets goes together on — to the open document, on their own 'Registration' cut layer (cutSide 'inside', no tabs). Positions are derived from the stock, not the drawing: `count` 3 (default) puts them in an L at the inset from three corners, which cannot be rotated or flipped onto itself, so a sheet only fits the pins the way it was cut; `count` 2 goes on the diagonal and does not stop a half turn. `diameterMm` defaults to a 3 mm pin, widened on a router to something the cut layer's tool can actually mill, and `insetMm` (default 5 mm) is how far the centres sit from the edges — inside the border a framed picture usually carries. Run it on every sheet of a layered piece with the same stock size and the same numbers and the holes land on the same millimetre each time, which is the whole point. Returns the new element ids and the hole centres; errors when the holes will not fit the stock, and notes when they land on existing artwork.
tools.etch_close_sheet: Close a sheet by `sheetId`, or the open one if none is given. Refuses to close the last sheet — there is always one open document. A closed sheet is gone: its drawing and its undo history go with it unless it was saved with etch_save_preset, so confirm with the user first.
tools.etch_combine: Combine two or more shapes into one path with a boolean operation: 'union', 'subtract', 'intersect' or 'exclude'. ORDER MATTERS — elementIds[0] is the base, and the shapes after it act on it, so 'subtract' cuts the later shapes out of the first one. The inputs are consumed, not hidden underneath (shapes left stacked under their own union would have every shared edge cut twice). Shapes with no closed outline — a line, an unclosed path — cannot take part; they are left in the drawing and named in the returned note. The result is a plain path with any rotation and scale baked in, at the position the shapes were drawn. Returns the new element's id, which of the inputs were consumed, and a note when anything needs saying — including when leftover pieces under 1 mm survived, which almost always means two edges were meant to line up and are a fraction of a millimetre apart.
tools.etch_delete_preset: Delete a saved user preset by name (with or without the 'user:' prefix). Built-in templates cannot be deleted. Destructive and not undoable — confirm with the user first.
tools.etch_erase: The eraser, by coordinate: lay a stroke of the given `width` (mm, default 2) along `points` (a list of {x, y} in mm, document space; one point is a round dot) and mask that band out of ONE layer's job — `layerId`, else the active layer. Nothing underneath is edited: the line is still a whole line and a photograph still has all its pixels, so deleting the returned element machines all of it again. Use it to hold a piece to the sheet by interrupting the cut around it, to drop part of a traced outline, or to blank an area of a shaded photo — never rewrite the geometry to do those, because the original is then gone. It masks that layer only: work on other layers running under the same stroke is untouched and still machined. Returns the new element's id, the layer it masks and the width.
tools.etch_export_svg: Export the active design as a clean, styled SVG XML string.
tools.etch_fill_region: The paint bucket, by coordinate: fill the region of the drawing that encloses the point (x, y) in mm, document space. The region is bounded by every visible line — closed shapes, open lines that meet, text outlines — and anything it encloses stays a hole. The result is one `path` element with machining 'filled' and hatchOutline false (the lines that bound it are already in the drawing), placed on the first fill layer, else the first etch layer, unless `layerId` is given. A gap in the outline narrower than 0.3 mm is sealed; a wider one is a doorway and the fill goes through it. Returns the new element's id, its area in mm², `openToStock` (true when the region reached the stock edge — the point was outside every closed shape and the background was filled, which is sometimes meant and sometimes an unclosed line) and `sealed`. Errors when the point is on a line or off the stock.
tools.etch_generate_gcode: Generate a GRBL/Marlin G-code toolpath for the active document — inner contours first, kerf-compensated, using the tool rack and machine settings currently loaded in the app. Options may override laserMode, spindleSpeedMax, travelSpeed and innerContourFirst. `options.removeOverlaps` (default true) makes a line two shapes share get cut once instead of twice; the returned program's header comments say how much doubled line was removed.
tools.etch_get_note_card: Return the active document's note card as { ok, markdown }. Empty string when the document has none.
tools.etch_get_schema: Return this reference: the document/element/layer schema, coordinate system, workflow and gotchas.
tools.etch_get_screenshot:
Capture the document as a PNG — the stock and everything on it, with the editing chrome (selection handles, node editor, guides) left out. The frame is the STOCK, not the viewport, so the picture does not depend on where the user has panned and two calls of the same document give the same image. scale is output pixels per mm (default 2, max 8): a 300x200mm sheet at scale 2 is 600x400. Returns { ok, dataUrl, width, height }.

Use it to check what you have drawn actually looks like the thing you meant — spacing, overlaps, whether text fits inside its border. Text is rendered with whatever font the browser has; an unusual face may fall back.
tools.etch_get_state: Return the full PhysBox: Etch state — document (dimensions, material, machine, layers, elements), selectedIds, activeTool and elementCount.
tools.etch_get_summary: The lightweight read of the document, and the one to reach for before etch_get_state. Returns the stock and material, every layer with its operation and element count, and one line per element: id, name, type, layer, and its position and size on the bed in mm (post-rotation, so it is the space the part actually occupies), plus the overall extent of the drawing. Carries none of the path data or embedded images that make etch_get_state large — a sheet with one photograph on it runs to megabytes there.
tools.etch_list_capabilities: List what this machine and build actually offer: the loaded tool rack (empty on a laser — that is how 'no tools to change' is expressed), the material catalogue, the layer operations, the four image modes, and the drawing tools in the UI. Also reports the boolean operations, the image dither modes and the document generators available in this build.
tools.etch_list_clipart: List the built-in vector clip-art symbols (id, name, category). They are line art designed to be machined, so prefer one over generating your own version of the same subject.
tools.etch_list_presets: List the built-in vector manufacturing presets (id, name, category, description). Returns built-in templates under `presets` and the user's own saved documents under `userPresets`, whose ids are of the form 'user:<name>'; either id can be passed to etch_load_preset.
tools.etch_list_sheets: List the sheets open in this job and say which one is being edited. Etch edits one document at a time and every other etch tool acts on the selected sheet, so call this before drawing when a job might have more than one — a layered picture is six sheets that share a stock size, a frame and a set of registration holes. Returns activeSheetId and, per sheet, its id, name, whether it is active, stock size, material, thickness, machine, element count and layer count. Sheets live for the browser session, like the open document itself: save each one with etch_save_preset to keep it.
tools.etch_load_preset: Load a built-in preset by id, replacing the entire active document. Ids: blank, hotel-keychain, mandala-coaster, intricate-mandala-art, box-joint-panel, spur-gear-set, wooden-desk-sign, cyberpunk-badge.
tools.etch_machine_arm:
Deliberately CANNOT arm the machine. It exists to give a clear answer rather than leave you guessing why motion is refused.

Arming is a click in the app, by the person standing next to the machine: ARM. If you need to move the machine and it is not armed, ask the user to click it — do not retry, and do not look for another route. The permission lasts about an hour and they can end it at any moment with DISARM in the same banner, which also cancels whatever is running.
tools.etch_machine_cancel: Stop the job and drop the rest of the program. Never gated. Soft-resets the controller, which leaves it in alarm if it was moving. The material has been cut into and generally cannot be registered again, so prefer etch_machine_pause if there is any chance of carrying on.
tools.etch_machine_connect:
Open the link to the machine. `transport` is 'usb' or 'wifi'; WiFi also needs `deviceId`.

USB opens a native port-picker that only the person at the keyboard can answer, so it only works if they are sitting there. WiFi has no such prompt.
tools.etch_machine_disarm: Give the permission back before it lapses, and stop anything running. Needs no arming itself.
tools.etch_machine_disconnect: Close the machine link. Does not stop a job — cancel or e-stop first if one is running.
tools.etch_machine_estop:
Emergency stop: soft-reset the controller and kill the beam, at once. Never gated and never refused.

Reach for this the moment something looks wrong — a cut in the wrong place, flame, the user saying stop. Position is lost and the machine needs re-homing, which is a small price. Do not deliberate about it.
tools.etch_machine_frame_job:
Trace the outline of the stock with nothing cutting, the guide beam lit. `guidePower` sets how bright. Needs the machine armed.

The check worth making before every job: is the stock where the job thinks it is, is it big enough, will the head foul a clamp. Seconds, and the operator can watch the outline land on the material. Do this after zeroing and before etch_run_job.
tools.etch_machine_goto_origin: Lift to a safe height, then travel to the work origin. Needs the machine armed.
tools.etch_machine_guide_spot:
Light the laser at pointer power so the operator can see where the head actually is. `on` defaults to true; `power` is a percentage. Needs the machine armed.

The most useful command in this set and the one with no equivalent in the other apps. Setting up a job by reading coordinates to someone is slow and error-prone; putting a visible dot on their material and asking "is that the corner?" is neither. Use it before etch_machine_zero_xy, and turn it off when done — starting a job turns it off anyway, since its S word would fight the program's own.
tools.etch_machine_home: Run the homing cycle ($H) against the limit switches. Needs the machine armed. Establishes machine coordinates; does not set the work origin.
tools.etch_machine_jog:
Move the head by a relative distance: x, y and z in mm, optional feedRate (default 1000). At least one axis required. Needs the machine armed.

On a laser, pair this with etch_machine_guide_spot: jogging blind and reading coordinates back is far worse than lighting the beam and asking the operator whether the dot is where they want it.
tools.etch_machine_list_devices: List the Tekno Boxes paired to this account, with whether each is online. Pass one of these ids as etch_machine_connect's deviceId to cut over WiFi. Read-only.
tools.etch_machine_pause: Feed hold: decelerate and stop without losing position or discarding the planner. Never gated — refusing a stop would be worse than having no permission system at all.
tools.etch_machine_probe_surface:
Probe a grid across the bed, for levelling a CNC job against stock that is not flat. Optional `cols`/`rows` (default 3x3) and `bounds`. Needs the machine armed.

Meaningless on a laser, which has no Z to compensate with. A 0.2mm dish across a 300mm bed is enough to cut through a 0.4mm veneer at one end and not scratch it at the other, which is what this is for.
tools.etch_machine_resume: Pick a paused job back up. Needs the machine armed.
tools.etch_machine_settings:
The controller's `$$` settings — max rates, accelerations, steps/mm — as read when the link opened. Read-only.

An empty result with a `note` means the controller never answered `$$`: the figures are unknown, not absent. This app's feed ceilings and time estimates come from these, and it says when it is falling back to an assumed profile.
tools.etch_machine_status:
Report the machine: whether it is connected, its GRBL state, work and machine coordinates, live feed and power, the trim percentages, and how far through a job it is. Read-only and never gated.

`armed` is the field that decides what else you can do. False means every command that moves an axis will be refused until the person at the machine allows it; `armedUntil` is when that permission lapses. The trim figures come from the controller's own status report, so they are right even if it was reset or adjusted from a pendant.
tools.etch_machine_trim:
Trim the running machine: `feed` and `spindle` take a step of 10, 1, -1 or -10 (percent) or 'reset'; `rapid` takes 100, 50 or 25. Never gated — it changes an already-running job without stopping it, where the alternative is aborting onto material that has been cut into and can no longer be registered.

This is what to reach for when a cut is scorching or a pass is not going through.

STEPS, NOT TARGETS: GRBL has no command to set a figure, so 87 is rejected rather than silently ignored. Nudge and check with etch_machine_status.
tools.etch_machine_unlock:
Clear GRBL's alarm lockout ($X). Needs the machine armed.

Routine after a boot lockout. NOT routine after a limit trip: the machine has lost its position and unlocking does not give it back. Home it before cutting.
tools.etch_machine_zero_xy:
Set the current XY position as the work origin — the corner the job is laid out from. Needs the machine armed.

This is the zeroing that matters on a laser, since there is no Z in the toolpath. Light the guide spot first and ask the operator to confirm the dot is on the corner of their material: that is a question they can answer, and "the DRO reads 12.4" is not.
tools.etch_machine_zero_z:
Set work Z0 where the tool is standing, with an optional `shimThicknessMm`. Needs the machine armed.

Deliberately not a probe: this app's CNC path touches off by hand or on a shim of known thickness. On a laser there is no Z in the toolpath at all, so there is nothing to zero toward and nothing to get wrong.
tools.etch_make_living_hinge: Cuts a living hinge into the open document: rows of slits that let a flat sheet bend. ADDS to the drawing; nothing already there is changed. The slits run along the axis the panel folds about, alternate rows are offset half a period so no uncut line runs straight across the hinge, and no slit comes within a beam's width of the edge of the region — a slit that reaches the edge is a split and the panel tears along it on the first fold. Options: x, y, width, height (the region, mm), axis ('x' folds about a horizontal line, 'y' about a vertical one), slitLengthMm, bridgeMm (the uncut torsion beam between slits in a row — under 1.2 mm is short grain in ply and a stress riser in acrylic), pitchMm (distance between rows; finer than the stock thickness and the beams twist badly). Every option may be sent as a number or as a numeric string. Returns addedIds, layerId, rows, slits and minBendRadiusMm — the tightest right-angle fold it will take, which is 2 x width / pi across the hinge. Errors when fewer than three rows fit, which is a crease rather than a hinge. All the slits arrive as ONE compound path element, not one per slit.
tools.etch_make_ornament: Draws a decorative pattern into a region of the open document. ADDS to the drawing; nothing already there is changed. `kind` picks the generator: 'guilloche' (the engine-turned rosette from a banknote or a watch dial, one continuous line), 'maze' (a perfect maze — exactly one route between any two points), 'animal_print' (tiger, zebra, leopard, cheetah or cow markings, traced as outlines), or 'foliage' (ornate vine scrollwork with curling tendrils and leaves). Region: x, y, width, height in mm, defaulting to the middle of the stock. Per-generator settings go in `options` and are validated against that generator's own field list — an option it does not have is an error naming the ones it does, rather than being ignored. Numbers may be sent as numeric strings. Everything a generator draws arrives as ONE compound path element. Guilloche, maze and foliage land on an etch layer; animal print lands on a CUT layer, so whatever its markings enclose falls out of the panel — move the layer to Etch first if the piece has to stay in one piece. Returns addedIds, layerId, operation and subpaths.
tools.etch_make_perforation: Fills a region of the open document with a field of holes: a speaker grille, a vent, a diffuser. ADDS to the drawing. Options: x, y, width, height (mm), lattice ('hex' staggers alternate rows and is the default because it leaves a wider web for the same open area, 'grid' is square), shape ('round' or 'slot'), sizeMm (diameter, or slot width), slotLengthMm, pitchMm (centre to centre), ramp ('none', 'linear' to fade across the region, 'radial' to fade outward — a grille that stops at a hard edge looks like it ran out of room). Numbers may be sent as numeric strings. Returns addedIds, layerId, holes, minWebMm and openAreaPercent. The web is the material left between two neighbouring holes and is the number that decides whether the panel survives: under 1 mm it tears out as the cutter passes. Past about 60% open area the sheet flexes and moves as it is cut. Holes are cut INSIDE the line so they come out the size asked for, and arrive as ONE compound path element.
tools.etch_make_test_grid: Generate a material test grid: one square per settings combination, on a scrap of the stock. REPLACES THE OPEN DOCUMENT — it is a job of its own, not an addition — but keeps the current stock size, material and thickness, since a test cut for the wrong material tests nothing. `options` accepts cols and rows (steps across and down), minSpeed/maxSpeed (mm/min, across), minPower/maxPower (laser: % of the tube; CNC: spindle RPM, down), cellSize and gap in mm, operation ('fill' for how dark or deep, 'cut' for whether it cuts through) and labels. Each cell gets its own layer holding explicit speed and power that override the derived feeds — including parts of the range the feeds model would refuse, which is the point of a sweep. Returns the size the grid needs and a warning when it will not fit the stock, since anything hanging off the edge is trimmed out of the toolpath and those cells come back blank.
tools.etch_new_sheet: Add a sheet to the job and switch to it. With `duplicate` true it is a copy of the open sheet, which is how sheet two of a layered piece gets its frame and its registration holes already in the right place; without it, a blank sheet that inherits this one's stock size, material, machine and layers, since a second sheet of the same job is cut from the same board. `name` names it — otherwise it follows the current name's numbering ('Sheet 3' → 'Sheet 4'). Returns the new sheetId and how many sheets the job now has.
tools.etch_run_job:
Cut the document that is open. Needs the machine armed. This is the one that cuts.

The program is generated from the same tool rack and settings the UI is showing, so what runs is what the operator is looking at. It refuses a document that produces no toolpath — usually layers with no operation assigned, or geometry sitting off the stock.

It also refuses if the machine is in alarm or a job is already running. The job stops by itself at every tool change; call etch_machine_status to see the pause, tell the user which tool, then etch_machine_resume.

Returns as soon as the job is streaming; poll etch_machine_status for progress.
tools.etch_save_preset: Save the current document as a user preset under a name, alongside the built-in templates. It is stored with everything the document carries, the note card included, so the description comes back with it. etch_list_presets returns it under userPresets with the id 'user:<name>', which is what etch_load_preset takes.
tools.etch_select_sheet: Switch to another sheet of the job, by `sheetId` (from etch_list_sheets) or by `index` (0-based, tab order). Everything else — adding elements, filling, erasing, generating G-code — acts on the selected sheet, so this is the call that decides where the next ones land. Each sheet keeps its own undo history; switching does not disturb it. Returns the new activeSheetId and its name.
tools.etch_set_document: Merge an EtchDocument (or any subset of its fields) onto the active document. Use for stock size, material, stockThickness, machine, gridSize, origin, layers, or to replace the whole elements array. Omitted fields are kept. The document's `notecard` can be set here too, but etch_set_note_card is the direct route and documents what a good card contains.
tools.etch_set_note_card:
Set the active document's note card — the markdown label shown on a card floating over the canvas. Call this on every document you build, and again when the design changes; nothing writes one for you, and a document without one arrives at the machine unlabelled. Unlike Mesh and Volt, whose cards are a positioned overlay array, Etch has exactly one card and it lives ON the document — so it is saved with a preset and comes back with it.

The markdown is the label for the piece, in the presets' house style (etch_load_preset one and etch_get_note_card to read it):
- `### Title` naming the actual object ("Vintage Hotel Key Tag").
- A bullet giving the finished size in mm and the stock it is cut from — material and thickness.
- A bullet per layer: what the operation is and what geometry sits on it.
- Any hole diameter, slot width, or spacing the maker would otherwise have to measure off the canvas.

Quote the numbers you placed the elements at, in mm.
tools.etch_set_svg: Import a raw SVG XML string onto the canvas, replacing the current elements and adding any layers the SVG implies. Returns importedCount and per-shape warnings.
tools.etch_update_element: Change one element in place: etch_update_element(id, updates), where updates holds any element fields (x, y, w, h, rotation, layerId, strokeColor, text, …). Prefer this over sending a whole elements array through etch_set_document, which discards anything that changed on the canvas between your read and your write. An element's id and type are identity, not properties — to change the type, delete it and add the replacement.
tools.etch_update_layer: Change one layer in place: etch_update_layer(layerId, updates), where updates holds any layer fields — name, color, operation ('cut' | 'etch' | 'fill' | 'shade' | 'ghost'), visible, locked, zDepth, passes, tool, cutSide, and the overrides (feedOverride, rpmOverride, stepdownOverride, speedOverride, powerOverride). Prefer this over sending a whole layers array through etch_set_document, which discards anything that changed on the canvas between your read and your write. Holding is here and is machine-specific: `tabs` (default true, router) leaves material at the bottom of a through-cut so the part stays put until snapped out; `bridges` (default false, laser) leaves short stretches of the outline unburnt, because a beam cannot leave a tab. With neither, a closed cut frees its piece — etch_generate_gcode's notes say what comes away and whether any of it carries engraving. A layer's id cannot be changed: elements are homed by it.
tools.etch_validate_document: Pre-flight the document and return { ok, problems, errorCount, warningCount }. Catches the faults that still export happily to G-code and only show up at the machine: geometry hanging off the stock (the machine drives to coordinates with no material under them), elements pointing at a layer that does not exist (no operation, speed or power — they never machine), elements on a hidden layer (hiding is a view setting, not an exclusion: they are still cut), sub-0.01mm strays from an accidental click, and a CNC cut layer whose zDepth is shallower than the stock, which scores instead of cutting through. Call it before etch_generate_gcode. ok is false only when there are errors; warnings are worth reading to the user.

document.name: string
document.origin: where machine X0 Y0 sits relative to the stock, e.g. 'top-left'
document.thickTabs: boolean — leave more material at each holding tab
document.defaultHatchAngle: number (degrees), applied when an element is switched to filled machining
document.notecard: markdown string — the piece's label, shown on a card floating over the canvas. Set it with etch_set_note_card on every document you build. Travels with the document into a preset and back out.

layer.name: string
layer.operation: 'cut' | 'etch' | 'fill' | 'shade' — shade machines an image as varying tone and takes only `image` elements
layer.speed: number (mm/min) — laser fallback when the material profile does not decide it
layer.zDepth: number (mm) — CNC only; ignored on a laser

elementCommonFields.name: string
elementCommonFields.hatchOutline: boolean — whether a filled element also cuts its outline

elementTypeFields.polygon: points (array of {x, y} in local mm); sides records how many the app generated
elementTypeFields.star: d (SVG path data); pointsCount, innerRadius, outerRadius describe the path the app generated
elementTypeFields.text: text, fontFamily, fontSize, fontWeight, letterSpacing, textPathId, textPathOffset, textPathAlign, textPathSide
elementTypeFields.symbol: symbolId (from etch_list_clipart); d and scaleX/scaleY are filled in from the library when omitted
elementTypeFields.bezier / freehand / path: bezierNodes (x, y, handleIn, handleOut) or d (SVG path data)
elementTypeFields.image: imageGray (base64 greyscale samples, one byte per pixel, row-major, 0 black), imgW/imgH (the sample grid), w/h (size on the material in mm), hatchSpacing (tone line pitch in mm), hatchAngle. Produced by etch_add_image in 'shade' mode — not something to hand-assemble.

gcodeOptions.laserMode: boolean — true for GRBL laser M3/M5, false for CNC Z-axis passes
gcodeOptions.spindleSpeedMax: number — maximum S value (e.g. 1000 on GRBL)
gcodeOptions.innerContourFirst: boolean — cut internal holes before outer boundaries
gcodeOptions.removeOverlaps: boolean, default true — cut a line two shapes share once rather than twice. A doubled laser line burns through thin ply where the rest of the outline does not; a doubled router pass sends the cutter full depth down a slot that is already air. Fills, shading, tabbed cuts and lines shared between two different layers are deliberately left alone.

imageOptions.threshold: 0-255 — what counts as dark. The first knob to turn when a trace comes back empty.
imageOptions.invert: boolean — for light artwork on a dark background
imageOptions.targetWidth: number (mm on the material); targetHeight is derived from the aspect ratio when omitted
imageOptions.shadePitch: number (mm between tone sweeps, shade mode) — a finer pitch costs proportionally more machining time
imageOptions.brightness: -100 to 100, a straight-line lift applied before thresholding
imageOptions.gamma: 0.2-3, default 1 — bends the middle greys without moving black or white. Above 1 lightens them, the usual fix for a photograph engraving too dark. Brightness and contrast cannot substitute: both are straight lines, so rescuing a scorched highlight with either also flattens the shadows that were already right.
imageOptions.dither: 'none' | 'floyd' | 'jarvis' | 'stucki' | 'ordered', SHADE MODE ONLY — turns the picture into pure black-and-white dots fired at one power, the way a newspaper prints a photograph. The answer for a machine that cannot hold a steady low power: a diode laser marks the same at 8% and 12%, so a photograph's shadows otherwise collapse into one flat grey. Floyd-Steinberg is sharpest, Stucki smoothest, 'ordered' a regular 8x8 pattern. Set shadePitch to the pixel size when using it (targetWidth divided by the traced pixel width, which is capped at 300 px on the long side) — a dithered picture IS its dots, and sweeping coarser samples them at random.
imageOptions.smoothing: boolean — fit curves to a traced outline instead of leaving the pixel staircase
imageOptions.simplifyPx: number (source pixels) — Douglas-Peucker tolerance on traced outlines
imageOptions.cutout: boolean, default false — cut the subject out of a plain white or black backdrop. The backdrop is flood-filled in from the picture's edges and removed; the edge of what remains becomes one closed path on the cut layer; the chosen mode applies to the subject alone. Anything the backdrop encloses is subject, so a white shirt on a white wall is kept.
imageOptions.cutoutBackground: 'auto' | 'white' | 'black' | 'any', default 'auto' — which backdrop to remove. 'auto' reads the median of the border pixels and picks white or black. 'white'/'black' are for when the edges of the picture are not backdrop. 'any' takes whatever colour the edges are and matches it in RGB rather than grey — for a photograph against a coloured wall; less certain, since anything the wall's colour goes with it.
imageOptions.cutoutTolerance: 0-255, default 0 (auto) — how far a pixel may differ from the backdrop and still be backdrop. Auto derives it from the spread of the border pixels, floored at 12 and capped at 96.
imageOptions.cutoutSmoothPx: integer source pixels, default 2 — radius of the open-then-close that removes hairs, dust and notches from the cut line before it is traced. A one-pixel spike is a whisker of material that breaks off.

machining.overview: Etch can drive the laser or CNC that cuts the document, not just design it. The tools are the etch_machine_* set plus etch_run_job.
machining.permission: Everything that can move an axis is refused until the person at the machine clicks ARM in the app. You cannot do this for yourself — etch_machine_arm exists only to say so. Reading state, trimming a running cut, pausing, cancelling and e-stopping all work without it, always.
order: 3. Ask the user to lay the material on the bed.
4. etch_machine_guide_spot on, then etch_machine_jog until the dot is on the corner they want, asking them — not reading coordinates at them.
6. etch_machine_frame_job and let them watch the lap.
gotchas: USE THE GUIDE SPOT TO SET UP. A visible dot on the material and "is that the corner?" is a question the operator can answer. Reading them coordinates is not, and it is how a job ends up cut 10mm off the edge.
A LASER HAS NO Z. There is no datum to get wrong and no probe before a job, which makes this app's setup much shorter than Volt's or Mesh's. Do not invent a zeroing step that does not apply.
FRAME BEFORE YOU CUT. It costs seconds and catches material that is too small, in the wrong place, or about to foul the head.
PREFER PAUSE TO CANCEL. A cancelled job leaves material that generally cannot be registered again.
DO NOT DELIBERATE ABOUT AN E-STOP. Flame is a real outcome on a laser. If the user says stop, call etch_machine_estop first and work out what happened afterwards.
